analysis.one_liner: Bans meatpackers from buying livestock through opaque, privately negotiated forward contracts, forcing open bidding and firm prices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without ever getting a vote, so packers kept using the pricing practices it would have restricted.
analysis.plain_summary: Large meatpackers buy a lot of cattle and hogs through "captive supply": private forward contracts signed weeks or months ahead, often with a formula price the seller cannot know on signing day. Because a handful of big packers control much of the buying, this lets them hold steady supplies of animals outside the open market, which ranchers say weakens the prices they can get at auction. S. 960 would have banned those arrangements: any forward contract would need a firm price set in dollars the day it was signed, would have to be offered through open, public bidding with multiple bids visible to buyers and sellers, could not use a formula price, and could not cover more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs. It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and hog farmers who sell livestock into open markets. With a firm base price set in dollars on the day they sign, open bidding they can watch, and a ban on opaque formula pricing, they would know what their animals are worth before committing them and would no longer be signing contracts whose price is set later by the buyer's own math. Consumers also have a stake: concentrated packer buying tends to squeeze producers, and fewer, larger buyers facing less competition can eventually show up in what shoppers pay.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that any forward contract between a producer and a packer carry a firm base price set as a fixed dollar amount the day the contract is signed, so a farmer knows what he is being paid before he commits the animals.

Requires forward contracts to be bid openly — with multiple bids solicited and buyers and sellers able to see the bids being made and accepted — instead of negotiated privately with one dominant buyer.

Bans formula pricing, where the final price is calculated later from a base the producer cannot see when signing, and caps the size of contracts a packer can use this way (over 40 head of cattle or 30 hogs would be off-limits under these contract types).
Leaves futures-market pricing and verifiable quality adjustments available, so hedging tools that work for both sides remain legal.

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies. Their ability to lock up livestock supply through privately negotiated formula contracts — "captive supply" — would have ended, forcing them to buy more animals through open bidding against other buyers. Some large-scale producers who prefer the convenience of long-term formula contracts would also have to change how they sell.

drawbacks.text: The contract limits are tight: a cattle forward contract covering more than 40 head, or a hog contract covering more than 30, would be prohibited, which could make it harder for large ranchers and hog operations to plan sales months ahead the way they do now.

Requiring firm base prices and open bidding removes the flexibility of formula pricing, which some producers used as a hedge; the bill tries to soften this by letting futures-market prices and verifiable quality adjustments stand, but packers and some large producers argued the rules would reduce available markets rather than create them.

Enforcement would run through the Packers and Stockyards Act's existing machinery, so the bill's value would depend on the Secretary of Agriculture actually policing the new rules — a constraint the bill does not itself change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a fairer, more transparent market for the ranchers and hog farmers who raise the animals, at the cost of some convenience for large-scale producers who like the current contract system and some compliance changes for packers. Critics could fairly argue that restricting contracts over 40 head could push packers toward fewer, bigger suppliers rather than helping small ones, and that formula contracts can also benefit producers by locking in volumes. On balance, the bill's open-bidding and firm-price requirements target a market where a handful of buyers set the terms, and the public interest in competitive livestock markets outweighs the packers' lost flexibility. The bill's main flaw was procedural: it was never seriously taken up, so none of it was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never came out, so the full Senate never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 28, 2005 and immediately referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
That referral was the last action ever taken: the record shows no hearings, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
It never got a vote despite bipartisan sponsorship — a Wyoming Republican leading the bill with Democratic and Republican cosponsors from farm states.

As a result, none of its contract rules — firm base prices, open bidding, a formula-pricing ban, contract size limits — ever became law, and packers could keep using the pricing practices it targeted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies, which kept their ability to buy cattle and hogs through private formula-priced contracts rather than open bidding. Ranchers and hog farmers gained nothing because the bill never became law.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican from Wyoming leading, with cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but because the bill never reached a hearing or a vote, the record shows no opposition votes or statements to measure the fight by.

industries.note: The bill outlaws the private formula-priced and forward contracts the big packers use to lock up livestock supply outside open markets. Losing captive supply means they would have to bid against each other in the open for cattle and hogs.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and hog farmers
industries.note: Producers selling into a market with open bidding and firm base prices get a real, visible price instead of an opaque formula. This is the group the bill was written for.

The bill explicitly excludes futures-based prices from its formula-pricing ban, so cattle and hog futures contracts remain a lawful, central pricing tool. This entrenches the futures market's role in livestock pricing.
